name: Load Shedding
intent: Survive overload by deliberately refusing some work early and cheaply, so the work you accept finishes in time and is still useful.
scenario: A service that can finish 100 requests per second normally receives 60. A spike sends 300 per second for 15 seconds. Clients give up after 2 seconds. With an unbounded queue the service stays 100% busy but almost nothing it finishes is still wanted, and it takes over a minute after the spike to recover.
problem: When arrivals exceed capacity, the excess has to go somewhere. A queue only turns missing capacity into delay. Once the delay exceeds the clients' timeout, the server spends all its capacity on requests whose callers have already left and retried, so throughput stays at 100% while goodput (answers delivered in time) falls towards zero. The collapse also outlasts the spike, because the backlog has to drain before fresh requests are served on time.

howItWorks.title: Separate throughput from goodput
howItWorks.text: Throughput is requests the server finishes; goodput is the ones whose caller was still waiting. Overload makes the two diverge. A queue of N requests adds N / capacity seconds of delay, so with capacity 100 per second and a 2 second timeout, any queue longer than about 200 produces answers nobody receives. Watch queue delay and goodput, not CPU, which sits at 100% in both the healthy and the collapsed state.

howItWorks.title: Refuse at the front when a limit is exceeded
howItWorks.text: Count requests in the system (queued plus running) and reject the next one above a limit with 503 Service Unavailable, or 429 Too Many Requests when you are pushing back on a specific caller, ideally with a Retry-After header (it tells the caller when to retry). Rejecting is fast and cheap, the caller learns immediately and can fail over, and everything admitted still finishes in time. By Little's law (requests in the system = arrival rate x time each spends there) the limit should be about capacity x acceptable latency: 100 req/s x 0.3 s gives roughly 30.

howItWorks.title: Let the limit find itself
howItWorks.text: A hand-picked limit goes stale when the service gets slower or faster. Adaptive limiters measure and adjust: AIMD (additive increase, multiplicative decrease) like TCP (add a little while latency is fine, cut by a factor such as 0.7 to 0.9 when it rises), or gradient limiters that compare the current latency with the best latency seen (Netflix concurrency-limits, Envoy adaptive concurrency). CoDel-style controllers watch queue delay instead and drop when it stays above a target (for example 5 ms in CoDel, a few hundred ms for an RPC service) for a whole interval.

howItWorks.title: Serve what is still useful, and what matters most
howItWorks.text: Under overload serve the newest request first (LIFO, last in first out, or adaptive LIFO that switches only when the queue is long): the oldest are the ones about to time out. Drop the oldest when the queue is full, and skip any request whose propagated deadline has passed instead of doing the work. Shed by priority: health checks, paying customers and writes that cannot be retried last; batch, prefetch and anonymous traffic first.

howItWorks.title: Shed as early and as cheaply as possible
howItWorks.text: Rejecting is not free: parsing, TLS and authentication cost CPU. Shed at the edge (load balancer, API gateway, the first middleware) before expensive work, and give each client a quota so one tenant cannot use all the capacity. This is different from rate limiting, which enforces a fair share all the time, and from backpressure, which slows the producer: load shedding is the emergency decision to drop work when the system as a whole has more than it can do.

pros: Keeps goodput near capacity during overload instead of letting it collapse
Bounds latency for the work you accept, because the queue is short
Recovery is immediate when the spike ends: there is no backlog of stale work to drain
Cheap rejections give callers an early, honest signal they can use to fail over or back off
cons: Some users get errors even though the system is up: you chose who loses
A static limit needs tuning and goes stale when the service or its dependencies change speed
Rejections still cost CPU, and with retrying clients they can themselves become the overload
Priority rules need classification at the edge and a policy someone owns, and can starve low priority traffic
Does not create capacity: sustained overload still needs scaling or a bigger service
whenToUse: Services with a hard capacity limit and clients with timeouts, which is nearly every request/response service
Traffic that can spike beyond what autoscaling can follow in time (it typically needs minutes)
Systems where some traffic is clearly more important than the rest, such as health checks, checkout or paid tiers
whenNotToUse: As a substitute for capacity planning or autoscaling: shedding for hours is an outage you chose
Where every request must eventually be processed and callers can wait: use a durable queue and backpressure instead
Where clients have no timeout and no way to handle a rejection, so a refusal is as bad as the delay it avoids
A service that never gets near its capacity and is not in a call chain with one that does
pitfalls: Limit set above capacity x client timeout (for example a queue of 400 at 100 req/s against a 2 s timeout), so accepted requests still time out
Clients that retry rejected requests at once, three tries each, turn 300 req/s into 700+ req/s and the rejections eat the capacity; honour Retry-After, use backoff with jitter and a retry budget
Shedding late, after authentication and parsing, so each rejection costs 20% of a request instead of about 1%
Returning 500 instead of 503 or 429, so clients and load balancers cannot tell overload from a bug, and breakers or alerts react wrongly
Shedding the health check, so the orchestrator restarts a healthy but busy instance and removes even more capacity
Serving requests whose deadline has already passed because the deadline is not propagated or checked
Critical traffic with no ceiling of its own, so it alone can fill the capacity, and no metric for how much was shed

roles.label: Clients
roles.description: Callers with a timeout. They give up after a deadline and may retry.

roles.label: Edge shedder
roles.description: Counts work in the system and rejects with 503 or 429 and Retry-After above the limit.

roles.label: Queue
roles.description: Holds admitted requests. Its length divided by capacity is the delay.

roles.label: Service
roles.description: Does the work at a fixed capacity, 100 requests per second here.

quiz.question: A service finishes 200 requests per second. Clients time out after 1 second and you want accepted requests to complete within about 250 ms. A spike sends 600 requests per second. Using Little's law, roughly what limit on requests in the system (queued plus running) is best?
options: About 600, so that nothing is turned away
About 200, matching capacity times the client timeout
About 400, matching the offered load over two seconds
About 50, capacity times the acceptable latency
quiz.explanation: Limit is about capacity times acceptable latency, which is 200 x 0.25 = 50. A limit of 200 lets accepted requests wait close to the full timeout, and larger limits mostly build answers that arrive after the caller has left.

quiz.question: A service is overloaded at 300 req/s against a capacity of 100. It returns 503 to excess requests, but clients retry immediately, up to 3 times. Offered load climbs past 700 req/s and even accepted requests slow down. What is the best fix?
options: Return 500 so clients treat the error as a bug and stop retrying
Honour Retry-After, back off with jitter, and cap retries
Hold rejected requests for one second before replying
Raise the limit to 300 so that nothing has to be rejected
quiz.explanation: Immediate retries multiply the load, so the rejections themselves become the overload. Clients need to back off with jitter and cap retries. Returning 500 does not stop retries and hides that this is overload, holding rejected requests for a second ties up the server and still invites a retry, and raising the limit above capacity brings back the queue.

quiz.question: A service with a 150-request queue handles 100 req/s and clients time out after 1 second. Served first-in first-out, every answer is already too late. No extra capacity can be added for the next few minutes. Which queue handling delivers the most useful answers?
options: Keep first-in first-out for fairness and ask clients to wait longer
Serve the oldest first and drop the newest arrivals
Serve newest first and skip requests past their timeout
Double the queue size so fewer requests are dropped
quiz.explanation: The oldest requests are the ones about to expire, so serving newest first (and skipping those past their deadline) turns capacity into answers people still want. First-in first-out under a deep queue spends everything on callers who have gone, and a bigger queue only adds more delay. Serving oldest first and dropping the newest keeps working on callers who are about to leave.
